title: pressure-scenario-lab-notes-sprint-45-2026
content:
Quick lab notes from the Pressure Scenario sync (Sprint 45). Mostly runbook/experiment scribbles and decisions we agreed to capture before followups.

Date: 2026-11-01
Attendees: Jordan Patel (owner), Priya Singh, Diego Ramirez, Lydia Park, Samir Gupta
Duration: 45m (standup-style + live run)

Agenda:
- Recap: recurring throughput dip at 80k qps across mixed seq workload
- Reproduce: synthetic pressure scenarios (priming vs cold path)
- Surface: any config/regression linked to recent kernel selector change (PR #4021)
- Next actions / runbook updates

Top-line summary:
- We reproduced a short ~30s throughput collapse when a microburst of short requests (avg seq_len 16) arrives concurrently with long requests (avg seq_len 512). Collapse appears as increased P99 latency and CPU throttling on the sidecar responsible for scheduling batches.
- Root hypothesis: kernel-selector fallback combined with aggressive batching heuristics causes head-of-queue batches to wait for long requests, creating a blocking window.
- Immediate mitigation agreed: gate the new selector behind a runtime flag and reduce batch_wait_ms from 8 -> 3 for mixed-seq routes.

Experiment notes (runs executed live):
1) Baseline (canary image: runtime:v2026-10-27)
   - Workload: mixed-seq 70/30 short/long, qps ramp 0 -> 80k over 60s, sustained 2m
   - Observed: P50 9ms, P95 42ms, P99 128ms, tail drops ~30s in with p99 spikes to 420ms, avg token throughput sustained but transient drop of 40% for 18s
   - Logs: saw batcher queue depth climb to 420, sidecar CPU at 87%

2) With kernel-selector v2 (runtime:v2026-11-01-pr4021)
   - Observed: earlier onset of p99 spikes (after ~12s), throughput drop longer (avg 26s), sidecar CPU pegged at 96% at peak
   - Notes: selector emitted repeated fallback logs: "kernel-mismatch -> soft-fallback", correlated with increased kernel compile traces in /var/log/runtime/compile.log

3) Reduced batch_wait_ms (8 -> 3) on same image as run 2
   - Observed: p99 reduced (median across runs) from 310ms -> 190ms during bursts, throughput collapse duration shortened to ~9s, sidecar CPU 78%
   - Tradeoff: small increase in small-batch overhead; agreeable for mixed workloads where latency SLO is primary.

4) Add prefix-KV warming (cache prefill) before burst
   - Observed: P99 tail further improved by ~20% vs run 3 when KV hit rate > 90%
   - Caveat: not always possible for customer traffic; good mitigation for known scheduled bursts (cron jobs)

Hypotheses and reasoning:
- H1 (primary): the kernel-selector's decision path tries to compile/choose a faster kernel for long sequences and holds batches open waiting for better packing; when mixed sequences arrive, this waiting increases head-of-line latency and batches are larger but blocked behind long seqs. Evidence: fallback logs and compile spikes during regressions.
- H2 (secondary): sidecar scheduling thread priority got lowered in the new build; we saw more CPU contention. Need perf counters to be sure.
- H3: network variance / NUMA mis-scheduling contributes to occasional stalls. Lower confidence.

Immediate action items (owners & due dates):
- Jordan: flip runtime feature-flag "enable-kernel-selector" -> off for prod canary until we validate selector heuristics (due 2026-11-02). Linked ticket SRV-1834.
- Priya: add a unit/integration test that simulates mixed-seq arrival patterns to our CI bench harness; target coverage before next release (due 2026-11-08).
- Diego: instrument sidecar with additional perf counters (sched latency, context-switches, kernel compile time) and push dashboard panels (due 2026-11-04).
- Lydia: run targeted NUMA-aware placement experiment across 3 different instance types and report differences (due 2026-11-06).
- Samir: Draft playbook entry for "mixed-request microburst" with rollback and mitigation steps (reduce batch_wait_ms, disable selector, KV warm) (due 2026-11-03).

Runbook / playbook edits (quick notes to add):
- New check: if batcher queue depth > 300 and p99 > 300ms -> auto-scale schedule to add dedicated batch workers; suggested control: bump worker_count +20% and reduce max_batch_size for short-route classes.
- Feature-flagging guidelines: any kernel-selector-like change must ship behind a flag and include opt-in trial on <5% traffic for 48h with synthetic mixed-seq shadow testing.
- Recovery steps for observed collapse: 1) toggle selector flag off; 2) set batch_wait_ms=3 for mixed routes; 3) prefill KV cache if possible; 4) roll back to last stable runtime image if no improvement in 10m.

Notes to self / loose ideas:
- Could we add a lightweight predictor that classifies in-flight requests into short/long within the first token and route them to different batch queues? Potentially avoids head-of-line waits. Prototype thought: use first-token classifier with <0.5ms overhead.
- Consider exposing batch_wait_ms per-route override from Console so SREs can tweak quickly on incident without rebuilds.

Logs & artifacts to attach to ticket SRV-1834:
- benchmarking-raw-run-2026-11-01.tar.gz (bench harness logs + metrics)
- sample-trace-ids: trace-9a3f, trace-b21c, trace-d44e (linked in run artifacts)
- runtime PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4021 (kernel selector)

Decisions made in sync:
- Block rollout of kernel-selector to >10% until we have mixed-seq shadow testing and a selector heuristic update.
- Short-term mitigation: reduce batch_wait_ms and add the playbook recovery steps.

Followups for next sync (2026-11-05):
- Status on flag flip and canary traffic metrics (Jordan)
- CI mixed-seq test merged (Priya)
- Dashboard panels live + initial perf counters (Diego)
- NUMA experiment results (Lydia)
- Playbook draft review (Samir)

Random notes (fragile/working):
- Observed correlation between compile logs and p99 spikes during run 2; investigate compile cache hit ratio.
- Might be worth running a binary that simulates "first-token classifier" locally on a small cluster to measure overhead.

End of notes. Save artifact in SRV-1834 and link to canary dashboard (internal link).

Editor note: informal doc. Will convert to a formal postmortem if a major regression is confirmed.
